docs.title: modeling-api
docs.text:
Labelled models · replayed preprocessing · typed, honest answers

Where the project is today: v0.2, the platform runs end to end on your laptop

make install && make dev && make seed starts the whole platform locally, without Docker: an HTTP API with an OpenAPI document, a job queue, a sandboxed runner, an object store that behaves like Google Cloud Storage, the web app and an isolated plot sandbox. From the browser, the CLI, the Python client or plain HTTP, you upload data, validate a spec as you type, fit it, follow the sampler live, inspect a signed model and score forecasts, new markets and what-ifs. The v0.1 contract layer (specs, 28 steps, 11 model plugins, plots, conformance corpus) still runs in your own Python process too. Cloud execution and multiple tenants come next: see the roadmap.

docs.title: Fit with preprocessing.Score with the same preprocessing.
docs.text:
modeling-api is a platform for Bayesian and classical models whose data has named dimensions: geo × channel × week, store × sku × day, household × trip. Describe a model in a small YAML spec or a few lines of Python. The platform checks your data, learns every preprocessing step on the training data only, and replays exactly that work whenever you forecast, add a new market or ask "what if".

Quickstart: 10 minutes Get started How it works

docs.title: Why labelled, multi-dimensional models?
docs.text:
Most model-serving stacks see a matrix: rows in, numbers out. Real business models do not live in a matrix.

What goes wrong with positional data

  • Column 7 used to be search spend; after a schema change it is social.
  • The forecast starts in week 53, but the lag features were built from week 1.
  • A market opens. Is it row 12? Does the model even know it is new?
  • Revenue was scaled by the mean, so the prediction came back in "1.37".
  • Someone sums the 90% quantiles of 40 stores and calls it the 90% quantile of the total.

What modeling-api does instead

  • Every array is an xr.Dataset with named dims and coordinates; nothing is positional, so shuffled, subset or reordered data scores the same.
  • Each dim declares what may happen at score time: fixed, extend (time) or new_levels (markets, stores, counties) with a declared strategy.
  • Every output says what it is: its representation (draws, quantiles, interval, point, moments), its units and its output space.
  • Requests that cannot be answered honestly fail before any compute, with a typed error code and a JSON pointer.

docs.title: The whole story in one picture
docs.text:
The same pipeline object runs at fit time and at score time. At fit time each step learns its state from the training data; at score time it replays that state. Steps that look back in time store a small per-group tail, so a forecast sees exactly the history the model was fitted on.

flowchart LR
    subgraph FIT["Fit (once)"]
        direction LR
        A["Daily spend & revenue<br/>local currency"] --> B["fx_convert<br/>(side table)"]
        B --> C["resample<br/>daily → weekly"]
        C --> S{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
        S --> D["mean_scale<br/><i>learns scale(geo, channel)</i>"]
        D --> E["lag_tensor<br/><i>stores last 6 weeks per geo</i>"]
        E --> M["model.fit"]
    end
    M --> BUN[("Bundle<br/>states · context tails · posterior<br/>hashes · no pickle")]
    subgraph SCORE["Score (any time)"]
        direction LR
        F["Next quarter's plan<br/>or a new market"] --> G["same steps,<br/><b>replayed</b> state"]
        G --> H["model.score"]
        H --> I["inverse → weekly EUR<br/>summaries · your names"]
    end
    BUN --> G
What you writeWhat the platform doesWhat you get back 
pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur, use: core.fx_convert@^1, with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, ...}}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1,   with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}
  - {id: scale,  use: core.mean_scale@^1, with: {vars: [spend], over: [time]}}
  - {id: lags,   use: core.lag_tensor@^1, with: {vars: [spend], along: time, within: [geo], l_max: 6}}
model:
  use: mmm.hierarchical_geo@^1.3
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit}
  1. Checks the whole spec statically: names, dims, settings, units at every stage, where the split happens and whether any step would learn from the holdout (LEAKAGE_RISK).
  2. Fits each stateful step on the training weeks only, fits the model, then scores the holdout through the same path a forecast uses and records the metrics.
  3. Refits on all weeks so forecasts start from the latest data, and writes a bundle with every state, context tail and hash.
  • Forecasts in weekly EUR, not "model units": scaling is inverted, and inversion stops at the weekly resample because daily values cannot be recovered from weekly sums. The output says so in its output_space attribute.
  • A new market drawn from the fitted hyperprior, honestly wider than a known one.
  • What-if deltas that share their noise with the baseline (common random numbers), so the delta reflects the change, not sampling noise.

docs.title: Safe by construction
docs.text:
• No pickle, anywhere

    Bundles are single zarr zips plus JSON sidecars. Native models are stored as skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON. Every file carries CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256, and reading verifies them.

  • Contracts are pure JSON

    mapi-spec never imports numpy or xarray, and the control plane never imports plugin code. Specs are validated from exported static JSON: settings schemas and schema effects. An import-linter contract enforces it.

  • Plots are sanitized

    Vega-Lite and Plotly specs are checked against pinned schemas. URL data, links, external images, tile maps, prototype keys and unsafe expressions are rejected before anyone sees a chart.

  • Typed errors, early

    UNSEEN_LEVELS, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT, MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE, CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED, … Stable codes, HTTP statuses and JSON pointers, raised before any compute is spent.

docs.title: Built for two kinds of people
docs.text:
• Guided: analysts

    Marketing and finance analysts pick a template, answer questions in business terms ("which column is revenue?"), enter priors as ROI ranges, and get a report with a sanity scorecard, plain-language captions on every plot and instant what-if sliders.

    Every plot recipe already ships a caption_plain and a persona, every model setting an x-ui-level, and every scorecard item a plain-language message. The Guided UI arrives in v0.4.

  • Expert: data scientists

    Write specs and plugins, inspect posteriors and preprocessing state, and pull any bundle into a notebook. The Expert web app, the mapi CLI and the Python client work today, and so does everything in plain Python.

    The Expert web app

  • Plugin authors

    A PyMC model is one build() method; an sklearn model is one estimator(). The contract kit tells you, before anyone runs your code, whether you followed the rules.

    Port a model

  • Integrators

    A versioned HTTP API with an OpenAPI 3.1 document, RFC 7807 errors, idempotency keys and server-sent events, plus a typed Python client. Endpoints, webhooks and MCP tools follow in v0.4.

    HTTP API guide

docs.title: What you get in v0.2
docs.text:
• The Expert web app

    Datasets, a YAML editor with live validation, live runs, a model inspector and scoring, with every plot in a sandboxed iframe. Web app guide

  • An HTTP API and its clients

    /v1 with OpenAPI 3.1, RFC 7807 errors, idempotency and SSE; the mapi CLI and a typed Python client. HTTP API

  • Sandboxed, verified runs

    A supervisor and worker per run, HMAC-signed events, outputs checked against the store's own checksums and a signed manifest. Security model

  • Runs on a laptop

    make dev without Docker (embedded PostgreSQL, a Cloud Storage emulator), or the same stack in containers. Deployment

  • Labelled data contract

    DataSchema, dim policies, roles, units, ragged layouts and plain-language data checks. Labelled data

  • Stateful pipelines

    28 built-in steps with fitted state, stages, splits, context tails and inverse transforms. Steps catalog

  • PyMC and scikit-learn

    nutpie, PyMC (segmented and resumable), MAP, ADVI; allow-listed sklearn and xgboost estimators with quantile, bootstrap and conformal uncertainty. Guides

  • Marketing-mix models

    A hierarchical geo MMM with response curves, marginal costs and a budget objective, and an adapter for pymc-marketing. MMM guide

  • Forecasting

    HSGP trends with horizon contracts, HMMs with terminal state and filtering. Time series

  • A conformance corpus

    Six reference problems run end to end on every change: validate, fit, score, evaluate, contract kit, plots. Corpus

docs.title: How it compares
docs.text:
MLflow and BentoML are excellent at what they target: packaging a trained model from almost any framework and serving it behind an API. modeling-api targets a narrower problem, labelled statistical models whose preprocessing, coordinates and uncertainty must survive the trip to production, and makes different trade-offs.

Tabular model serving (MLflow / BentoML style) modeling-api Input contract Column or tensor signatures: names and shapes, no dimensions xr.Dataset with named dims, coordinates, roles, units and per-dim score policies Preprocessing at score time Up to you: bundle it into the model artifact, or re-implement it in the service Declared steps with fitted state, replayed exactly; stage-aware splits and per-group context tails New groups and horizons Whatever the model happens to do with an unseen row Declared per dim (fixed, extend, new_levels + strategy); checked before compute Uncertainty Point predictions by default; intervals are a custom output A first-class representation that decides which summaries and aggregations are valid Units of the answer Whatever space the model was trained in Inverted to original units, with the output space recorded on every variable Serialization Framework-native; pickle and cloudpickle are common Zarr zip + JSON, skops or xgboost JSON; pickle is rejected on write and on read Validating a request At call time, inside the model Statically, from JSON, before a run starts: typed errors with JSON pointers Who it is for Any model, any framework Bayesian and classical models of panels, time series and hierarchies; analysts and data scientists

docs.title: A taste
docs.text:
The same model in plain Python, without any server. The Python guide builds it end to end; every snippet on this site is executed by the test suite.

from mapi_sdk import fit_spec

bundle = fit_spec(spec, data, registry=registry, raw_schema=schema)
print(bundle.metrics.values)  # holdout metrics, in units sold: {'rmse': ..., 'mape': ..., ...}
print(bundle.metrics.n_holdout)  # 48 cells: 3 stores x 2 skus x 8 weeks

from mapi_spec import ErrorCode, MapiError


def try_score(request_yaml: str, payload: xr.Dataset) -> ErrorCode:
    try:
        score_bundle(bundle, request_yaml, payload, registry=registry)
    except MapiError as err:
        print(err.code, "-", err)
        return err.code
    raise AssertionError("expected a typed error")


FORECAST = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
"""

# 1. a forecast without next month's promotions: promo is future_required
code_1 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.drop_vars("promo"))

# 2. quantiles are per cell, so "total over all stores" would be a made-up number
code_2 = try_score(FORECAST + "output: {aggregate: {over: [store]}}\n", plan)

# 3. a product outside the fitted range: sku is a fixed dim
code_3 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.assign_coords(sku=["apples", "kiwis"]))

  • Next: run the platform and fit your first model

    Quickstart

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
modeling-api is built from a few ideas that fit together. Each page in this section explains one of them with code you can run.

flowchart TB
    subgraph CP["Contracts — mapi-spec (pure JSON, no numpy)"]
        direction LR
        SCH["DataSchema<br/>dims · policies · roles"]
        SPEC["ModelSpec<br/>pipeline · model · split"]
        REQ["ScoreRequest<br/>mode · horizon · output"]
        CAT["Catalog<br/>settings schemas · schema effects · manifests"]
        VAL["Static validation<br/>stages · leakage · CoordPlan"]
    end
    subgraph RT["Runtime — mapi-sdk (xarray)"]
        direction LR
        PIPE["Pipeline<br/>fit → state · transform · inverse"]
        PLUG["Model plugin<br/>fit · score"]
        COORD["Coord canonicalisation"]
        SUM["Summariser<br/>representation-aware"]
        BUN[("Bundle")]
    end
    SPEC --> VAL
    SCH --> VAL
    CAT --> VAL
    REQ --> VAL
    VAL -->|"resolved spec"| PIPE
    PIPE --> PLUG --> BUN
    BUN --> COORD --> PLUG
    PLUG --> SUM

The split between the two halves matters. The contracts are JSON in, JSON out; the platform's API depends only on them, so it can validate any spec and any score request without importing your code or decoding your arrays. The runtime touches arrays and runs plugins; it lives in notebooks and in the sandboxed runner. How the platform puts the two halves together is in the Architecture overview, and what keeps it safe in the Security model.

docs.title: The ideas
docs.text:
• Labelled data

    Data is an xr.Dataset. A DataSchema gives each dim a policy (fixed, extend, new_levels) and each variable a role, units and missingness rules. Bindings map your names to a model's canonical names and back.

  • Pipelines and stages

    Steps learn state on train and replay it at score time. The split happens at a named stage; look-back steps store per-group context tails; inverse transforms stop at the last reshape and record the output space.

  • Representations and summaries

    Draws, quantiles, intervals, points and moments. The representation decides which summaries exist and which aggregations are honest.

  • Bundles

    The fitted artifact: one zarr zip plus JSON sidecars, every file hashed, no pickle.

  • Coord plans and typed errors

    Score requests are checked against the fitted coordinates before any compute: unseen levels, horizons, gaps, missing future covariates, impossible summaries.

  • Capabilities and manifests

    What a model declares about itself, statically: representation, score modes, outputs, derived quantities, which preprocessing it owns.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Canonical name The name a step or model uses (geo, time, y). data.bind maps it to your dataset's name (market, date, revenue). Stage The dataset after a named step. raw is the bound input. Splits, context and scenario entry points (inputs_stage) all refer to stages. Step state What a step learned at fit time: JSON plus labelled arrays (for example scale(geo, channel)), and a context tail for look-back steps. Never written into the spec. Score The umbrella term for "predict with replayed preprocessing". Modes: predict, forecast, counterfactual, simulate, filter, evaluate. Representation How a model encodes uncertainty: draws, quantiles, interval, point or moments. Output space Where an output's values live after inversion, for example raw or weekly. Bundle The verified result of a fit: states, model groups, native artifacts, manifest and hashes. Run A unit of work (fit, score, …) submitted to an executor as JSON.

docs.title: Architecture overview v0.2
docs.text:
modeling-api is three layers, built in this order: a typed modelling runtime (the SDK, the steps and the model plugins), a job platform around it (the API, the queue, the executors and the runner), and, from v0.3, a hosted multi-tenant platform. The rules that make the last one safe hold from the first: the control plane never imports plugin code and never decodes your arrays, every run happens in a sandbox, and every output is checked against what the storage itself computed.

flowchart TB
    subgraph clients["Clients"]
        web["Web app<br/>(app origin)"]
        sandbox["Plot sandbox<br/>(separate origin)"]
        cli["mapi CLI · Python client ·<br/>curl · other apps"]
    end
    subgraph control["Control plane: JSON only, never imports plugins"]
        api["API<br/>/v1 · OpenAPI · SSE"]
        orch["Orchestrator<br/>dispatcher · reconciler ·<br/>finalizer · event ingestion"]
        pg[("PostgreSQL<br/>runs · queue · events ·<br/>registry · catalog")]
    end
    subgraph exec["Run sandbox: one per run"]
        sup["Supervisor<br/>(trusted, holds the run's URLs)"]
        wrk["Worker<br/>(untrusted: SDK + plugin)"]
    end
    store[("Object store<br/>quarantine · bootstrap · runs ·<br/>bundles · data")]

    web -->|"/v1"| api
    cli -->|"/v1"| api
    web -. "postMessage<br/>(validated)" .-> sandbox
    web -->|"signed PUT / GET"| store
    api --> pg
    orch --> pg
    api -->|"metadata, signed URLs"| store
    orch -->|"bootstrap object,<br/>verify, server-side copy"| store
    orch -->|"submit(run id, nonce)"| sup
    sup <-->|"socketpair"| wrk
    sup -->|"signed URLs only"| store
    sup -->|"HMAC-signed events"| orch

docs.title: The control plane
docs.text:
The API and the orchestrator share one PostgreSQL database. The API writes runs in state created and decides queued or rejected from static checks; everything after that belongs to the orchestrator.

flowchart LR
    subgraph api["API process"]
        routes["/v1 routes"]
        validate["Static validation<br/>(SchemaEffect JSON,<br/>CoordPlan, sanitizers)"]
        sse["SSE fan-out<br/>(one LISTEN per process)"]
    end
    subgraph worker["Worker process"]
        disp["Dispatcher<br/>token bucket · intent row"]
        rec["Reconciler<br/>every 10 s"]
        ev["Event ingestion<br/>HMAC verify · dedupe"]
        fin["Finalizer<br/>(procrastinate job)"]
    end
    pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    routes --> validate
    routes -->|"runs, specs,<br/>datasets"| pg
    disp -->|"lease queued runs"| pg
    rec -->|"executor status →<br/>state transitions"| pg
    ev -->|"run_progress upsert,<br/>run_events + NOTIFY"| pg
    fin -->|"model versions,<br/>signed manifests"| pg
    pg -->|"NOTIFY"| sse
  • Static validation runs in the API, synchronously, from JSON only: each step's exported schema effect and each model's settings schema and schema template, taken from the catalog. The catalog is produced by a sandboxed describe run of the real runner and cached per image digest, so the API validates against exactly what the runner will execute.
  • The dispatcher leases queued runs through a token bucket, writes an intent row (run, attempt, nonce) and then calls the executor, so a crash between the two can be recovered.
  • The reconciler is level-triggered: every 10 seconds it compares each active run with the executor's own status, which is the source of truth for liveness. Silence only marks a run stalled; an execution that vanished is retried as a new attempt (within a cost window), and orphaned executions are adopted by their nonce.
  • The finalizer turns a finished execution into a model version (see Storage and integrity).
  • Events are verified, deduplicated on (run, attempt, seq), and stored as one run_progress row per run plus run_events for state changes, warnings, diagnostics and metrics. A PostgreSQL NOTIFY wakes the SSE streams of every API process.

The state machine, every transition and who owns it are in the Run protocol.

docs.title: The run sandbox
docs.text:
Every run, whatever its kind (ingest, describe, validate, fit, score), gets a fresh pair of processes: a trusted supervisor and an untrusted worker.

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Dispatcher
    participant S as Object store
    participant X as Executor
    participant R as Supervisor
    participant W as Worker (SDK + plugin)
    D->>S: PUT bootstrap/{nonce}: RunSpec (signed URLs, HMAC key, limits)
    D->>X: submit(MAPI_RUN_ID, MAPI_NONCE)
    X->>R: start (no secrets in argv or env)
    R->>S: GET bootstrap/{nonce}, then DELETE it
    R->>S: GET inputs (signed, generation-pinned, CRC32C-checked)
    R->>W: spawn: scrubbed env, separate uid (where possible), python -I
    W-->>R: progress, logs, results (framed JSON over a socketpair)
    R-->>D: stdout: one HMAC-signed event per line
    R->>S: POST outputs (V4 POST policy on the attempt prefix)
    R->>S: PUT manifest.json (signed claim of every object)
    R-->>D: "complete" event, exit 0
  • No credentials in the environment. The executor passes only MAPI_RUN_ID and MAPI_NONCE. The run's signed URLs and its event HMAC key are in a one-time bootstrap object that the supervisor reads and deletes before any model code starts.
  • The worker is untrusted. It runs the SDK harness and the plugin with an allow-listed environment (every MAPI_* removed), in its own session, under uid 10001 with no_new_privs when the supervisor runs as root (containers, Cloud Run). It talks only to the supervisor, through length-prefixed JSON frames that must match their schemas.
  • Only the supervisor writes events. Its stdout carries one JSON event per line, each with a sequence number and an HMAC; anything the worker prints becomes a capped, control-character-stripped log event.
  • Caps everywhere. Log lines (4 KB) and total logs (20 MB), event size, output objects and bytes, and a scratch budget per resource class. Breaking one is a SANDBOX_VIOLATION or RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, never a silent truncation of results.
  • Checkpoints. On SIGTERM or near the deadline, a PyMC fit flushes its last segment and the supervisor uploads a partial manifest; the run can be resumed from there.

On a laptop the worker cannot change user, so runs report DEV_MODE_ISOLATION: the process split, the scrubbed environment, the event signing and the output verification all still apply, but the worker runs as you. See the security model.

docs.title: Storage and integrity
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph buckets["Buckets: mapi-{env}-*"]
        q["quarantine<br/>uploads, 7-day lifecycle"]
        b["bootstrap<br/>one-time RunSpecs"]
        r["runs<br/>attempt scratch"]
        bun["bundles<br/>write-once, retention lock"]
        d["data<br/>content-addressed datasets"]
    end
    browser(("browser /<br/>client")) -->|"signed PUT"| q
    q -->|"signed GET"| ingest["ingest run"]
    ingest -->|"POST policy"| r
    r -->|"verify, then<br/>server-side copy"| d
    fit["fit / score run"] -->|"POST policy"| r
    r -->|"verify, then<br/>server-side copy"| bun
    bun -->|"signed GET, minted after<br/>the manifest signature checks"| client(("client"))
Bucket Who writes Who reads quarantine Browsers and clients, through a signed PUT for one object Ingest runs, through a signed GET bootstrap The dispatcher The supervisor, with a principal that may get and delete there and nothing else (no list) runs Runs, through a POST policy limited to their attempt prefix and a size range The finalizer (metadata) bundles The finalizer only, by server-side copy; write-once under a retention lock Clients and runs, through signed GETs minted after verification data The finalizer, by server-side copy of ingest outputs Runs, through signed GETs

Outputs are claims. When a run ends, the finalizer lists the attempt prefix and reads each object's metadata: the size, CRC32C, MD5 and generation the store computed. It compares them with the run's signed manifest and refuses missing, changed or unexpected objects (INTEGRITY_FAILURE). It validates the small JSON sidecars under size caps, sanitizes the plots, copies the verified generations into the bundles bucket, and signs a bundle manifest that binds the tenant, run, spec hash, data hash, catalog digest and every destination generation (an EC P-256 key locally, standing in for Cloud KMS). Every later download link is minted only after that signature checks, so a swapped object can never be served. Bundles themselves are zarr zips plus JSON: nothing is pickled.

docs.title: The event path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["Worker"] -->|"frames"| S["Supervisor"]
    S -->|"stdout:<br/>{mapi_event, hmac}"| P{{"local executor:<br/>stdout pipe"}}
    S -.->|"v0.3: Cloud Logging<br/>→ Pub/Sub push"| I["POST /internal/events"]
    P --> V["Verify HMAC ·<br/>dedupe (run, attempt, seq)"]
    I --> V
    V -->|"progress: upsert"| RP[("run_progress")]
    V -->|"state, warning, diagnostic,<br/>metric, complete, error"| RE[("run_events")]
    RE -->|"NOTIFY"| SSE["SSE streams<br/>Last-Event-ID resume"]
    RP --> SSE
    SSE --> C(("web app ·<br/>CLI · client"))

Locally the executor reads events straight from the supervisor's stdout. In the cloud the same lines travel through Cloud Logging and Pub/Sub to POST /internal/events; the verification is the same. Progress is coalesced to one event every couple of seconds and kept as a single row, so a long fit does not write thousands of rows; only state changes, warnings, diagnostics, checkpoints, metrics and terminal events are persisted and replayed to a reconnecting client.

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
A bundle is everything a fit produced that scoring needs, in a form that is safe to store, move and read back: one bundle.zarr.zip plus four JSON sidecars.

fruit-demand-v1/
├── bundle.zarr.zip      # one zarr v3 zip: the whole fitted model as an xr.DataTree
├── manifest.json        # identity, provenance, lineage and the hashes of every file
├── metrics.json         # holdout metrics (computed through the score path)
├── diagnostics.json     # convergence and sanity checks, expert and plain-language
├── plots.json           # rendered, sanitized plots for outputs.plots
└── evaluation/          # evaluate_then_refit: the train-only bundle behind the metrics

docs.title: Write, read, verify
docs.text:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from mapi_sdk import Bundle

out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "fruit-demand-v1"
manifest = bundle.write(out)
print(sorted(p.name for p in out.iterdir()))
# ['bundle.zarr.zip', 'diagnostics.json', 'evaluation', 'manifest.json', 'metrics.json',
#  'plots.json']  - `evaluation/` is the train-only fit that produced the holdout metrics

again = Bundle.read(out, registry)  # every file's size and hashes are verified here
assert again.bundle_id == bundle.bundle_id

Bundle.read recomputes the size, CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256 of every file and compares them with the manifest. A damaged or tampered bundle raises BundleError (INTEGRITY_FAILURE).

docs.title: What is inside
docs.text:
print(manifest.role, manifest.plugin["id"], manifest.spec_hash[:19])
# production tabular.regressor sha256:...
print(manifest.files["bundle.zarr.zip"])  # size, crc32c, md5 (GCS forms) and sha256
print(manifest.lineage["evaluation_bundle"])  # the train-only fit behind the metrics

tree = again.to_tree()  # the whole bundle as one xr.DataTree
print(sorted(tree.children))
# ['binding', 'fit_coords', 'model', 'native', 'preprocess', 'schema', 'spec']
print(sorted(tree["preprocess"].children))  # ['cal', 'logy']: one node per step
Node Holds /spec The canonical spec and the resolved spec (pinned versions, every stage's schema) /schema/raw, /schema/model The data contract at the input and at the model stage /binding Canonical ↔ dataset names, reversed on every output /preprocess/<step> Each step's learned JSON state, labelled arrays and per-group context tail /model The manifest, settings, fit config and learned JSON /model/<group> ArviZ-named groups: posterior, sample_stats, log_likelihood, observed_data, … /terminal_state Sequential models: the filtered state at the last fitted step /native Safe native artifacts: skops files, xgboost JSON, … /derived/<name> Derived quantities cached at fit (contributions, response curves) /fit_coords/<stage> The fitted coordinates at every stage (what CoordPlan checks against) /side_tables/<name> pinned side tables, frozen with the fit /thin The bundle-wide thinning index for draws

docs.title: No pickle, ever
docs.text:
Pickle executes code when it is loaded, so it has no place in an artifact that moves between users, services and sandboxes.

  • Model groups are labelled arrays in zarr; settings, states and manifests are JSON.
  • Native estimators are stored as skops (loading lists the file's types first and refuses anything outside that estimator's allow-list) or xgboost JSON.
  • FitOutput.native entries that look like pickle (.pkl, .joblib, .pt, pickle magic bytes, …) are rejected when a bundle is written and when it is read. The contract kit checks it for every plugin.

docs.title: Hashes in the forms object stores report
docs.text: CRC32C and MD5 are recorded base64-encoded, the way Google Cloud Storage computes them on upload. The platform binds a signed manifest to the object generations and server-computed hashes, so an uploaded artifact cannot be swapped or replayed (see Storage and integrity). SHA-256 is recorded too, for content addressing.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
The manifest records the spec hash, the data hash, the plugin and every step version, and the library versions a bundle was fitted with; manifest.lineage links a production bundle to its evaluation bundle. "Which data and which code made this forecast?" always has an answer.

Next: Coord plans and typed errors.

docs.title: Capabilities and manifests
docs.text:
A model plugin describes itself with a manifest: static JSON that says what data it needs, what it can do, what it returns and which settings it takes. The control plane validates specs and score requests against manifests, and the Guided UI builds its forms from them, all without ever importing the plugin.

from mapi_sdk import default_registry

registry = default_registry()
manifest = registry.model("mmm.hierarchical_geo@^1").manifest()
caps = manifest.capabilities

print(caps.representation.value, caps.inference)  # draws mcmc
print(sorted(caps.score_modes))
# ['counterfactual', 'evaluate', 'forecast', 'predict', 'simulate']
print(caps.decision, caps.contribution_scale)  # True additive
print([d.name for d in manifest.derived])  # ['contributions', 'response_curves', 'marginal_cost']

basic = [k for k, v in manifest.settings_schema["properties"].items() if v.get("x-ui-level") == "basic"]
print(basic)  # ['pooling', 'adstock', 'saturation']: what Guided mode shows

adapter = registry.model("mmm.pymc_marketing@^1").manifest().capabilities
print(sorted(adapter.owns))  # ['carryover', 'inverse_units', 'scaling']

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Field Meaning inference mcmc, vi, map, smc, kalman, point, bootstrap or custom representation draws, quantiles, interval, point or moments. See Representations score_modes Which of predict, forecast, counterfactual, simulate, filter, evaluate the model supports. Anything else is MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED decision Has an objective(fitted, decision) returning a value per draw, for budget optimisation recommend Can recommend candidates (Bayesian optimisation) fast_score Provides a compiled fast-scoring path (PyMC FrozenPredictor) contribution_scale additive (contributions sum to the prediction; the contract kit checks it), multiplicative or none loo_valid, loo_invalid_reason Whether pointwise LOO is meaningful. An HMM's steps are dependent, so ts.gaussian_hmm declares it invalid and elpd_loo is rejected at validation identified_quantities Which parameters are identified (for models with label switching or rotations) owns Preprocessing the model does itself: scaling, carryover, inverse_units, recursion. The platform steps aside and labels outputs accordingly deterministic_given_seed Whether the same seed gives the same fit (nutpie: no). The contract kit checks it when claimed checkpointable Long fits can be checkpointed and resumed

docs.title: The manifest
Steps have manifests too
docs.text:
Each step exports a catalog entry: its settings JSON Schema, kind, whether it is stateful or invertible, which settings name variables, dims and side tables, its context need, and a schema effect template. The runner images export the catalog when they are built, and the API validates specs against it. Browse it in the steps catalog.

python -m mapi_steps.catalog --splits > catalog.json   # what the control plane loads

docs.title: Browse the built-ins
docs.text:
• Models catalog: every installed model's capabilities, outputs, derived quantities and settings.
  • Plot recipes catalog.
  • Spec schema: every field of ModelSpec and ScoreRequest.

docs.title: Coord plans and typed errors
docs.text: Before a score request touches a model, its coordinates are checked against what the model was fitted on. The checks are called the CoordPlan, and almost all of them need only metadata: the fitted coordinates of every stage (stored in the bundle) and the request itself. That is why the API can reject a bad request in milliseconds, without starting a sandbox.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text:
Code HTTP Raised when What to do UNSEEN_LEVELS 422 A label of a fixed dim (or a new_levels dim with strategy error) was not in the fit Drop it, or declare the dim new_levels with a strategy and refit COORD_NOT_ALLOWED 422 An extend dim starts before the fitted range, or a label cannot exist Send labels inside or right after the fit NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION 422 New time labels leave a gap after the fitted range Send the missing periods (context tails need them) HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT 409 The forecast reaches past max_extension Refit with a larger max_extension MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE 422 A future_required variable is missing over the horizon Supply it in the payload CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED 422 The output asks for something the representation cannot give (summing quantiles, draws from a point model, an HDI from quantiles) Ask for a valid summary, or use a model with joint draws RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED 422 A target lag shorter than the horizon Use longer lags or a model that owns recursion MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED 422 The model does not declare the requested mode See the model's capabilities SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE 422 A side table does not cover the periods a step needs Supply a table that covers them

HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT is a 409, not a 422: the request is fine, the model is not ready for it. The fix is a refit, not a different request.

docs.title: Metadata only: what the API checks
docs.text:
from mapi_sdk import CoordPlan
from mapi_spec import load_score_request, validate_score_request

# What the API stores next to a model version: JSON only, no arrays, no plugin code.
meta = CoordPlan(load_score_request(FORECAST), bundle.resolved, bundle.fit_coords).metadata()
print(f"{len(meta.model_dump_json()) / 1024:.0f} KiB of metadata")

request = load_score_request(FORECAST + "output: {summary: [hdi_90], draws: 100}\n")
for issue in validate_score_request(request, meta):  # no data, no model: milliseconds
    print(issue.code, issue.pointer, "-", issue.message)
# MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE /data - forecasting needs future values of ['price', 'promo'] ...
# CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED /output/draws - draws were requested but the model's
#                                        representation is 'quantiles'
# CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED /output/summary/0 - summary 'hdi_90' cannot be computed from
#                                            'quantiles' output

Every problem is reported at once, each with a JSON pointer into the request. The metadata is a few kilobytes of JSON per model version; no arrays are decoded and no plugin code is imported.

docs.title: In the runtime: the same checks, then canonicalisation
docs.text:
score_bundle runs the same checks against the real payload (so it can also see which values are present), raises the most specific error, and keeps the remaining notices (for example "1 new level of store will use strategy pooled") in the output's issues attribute.

from mapi_spec import ErrorCode, MapiError


def try_score(request_yaml: str, payload: xr.Dataset) -> ErrorCode:
    try:
        score_bundle(bundle, request_yaml, payload, registry=registry)
    except MapiError as err:
        print(err.code, "-", err)
        return err.code
    raise AssertionError("expected a typed error")


FORECAST = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
"""

# 1. a forecast without next month's promotions: promo is future_required
code_1 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.drop_vars("promo"))

# 2. quantiles are per cell, so "total over all stores" would be a made-up number
code_2 = try_score(FORECAST + "output: {aggregate: {over: [store]}}\n", plan)

# 3. a product outside the fitted range: sku is a fixed dim
code_3 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.assign_coords(sku=["apples", "kiwis"]))

Then it canonicalises the model-stage data, so a plugin never has to reason about request order or new labels:

  1. Reorder every fixed and new_levels dim to the fit order. Posterior arrays are indexed by position, so county_03 must sit where it sat at fit time.
  2. Pad requested subsets out to the full fitted set (masked), so shapes match the fit.
  3. Append new levels after the fitted ones, flagged by a boolean coordinate <dim>__is_new; <dim>__requested marks real (non-padding) labels.
  4. Call plugin.score(...).
  5. Select the requested labels back, in request order, and drop the helper coordinates.
flowchart LR
    R["request: county_07, county_02, county_new"] --> O["fit order<br/>county_00 … county_07"]
    O --> P["+ county_new<br/>county__is_new = True"]
    P --> S["plugin.score"]
    S --> B["select back:<br/>county_07, county_02, county_new"]

Inside a plugin, mapi_sdk.new_level_mask(ds, "county") returns the __is_new flags and ScoreContext.strategy("county") the effective new-level strategy. PyMC models get all of this for free through ctx.hier_effect(...); see Bring a PyMC model.

docs.title: Errors are values, not strings
docs.text:
Every error is a MapiError with:

  • a stable code (an ErrorCode) and an HTTP status;
  • a platform-written detail, and the list of issues behind it, each of which can carry a suggested_action;
  • a JSON pointer to the offending field;
  • untrusted_text: anything a dataset or plugin said, kept apart from the message so a UI can render it as plain text and an agent can treat it as data, never as instructions.

Over HTTP an error is an RFC 7807 problem document. The full list is in Error codes.

Next: Capabilities and manifests.

docs.title: Labelled data
docs.text:
Every model on modeling-api reads one xr.Dataset: variables with named dims, and dims with coordinate labels. Nothing is positional, so the platform can reorder, subset, extend and add labels safely, and you can score data whose stores are in a different order than at fit time.

A DataSchema describes such a dataset: what each dim is and what may happen to it at score time, and what each variable means to a model.

docs.title: A schema in one look
docs.text:
layout: dense                       # or: long (one row per observation + *_idx variables)
dims:
  market:  {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
  channel: {kind: categorical, policy: fixed}
  date:    {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: D}
vars:
  revenue: {dims: [market, date], dtype: float64, role: target, units: EUR}
  spend:   {dims: [market, channel, date], dtype: float64, role: spend, units: EUR,
            future_required: true}

docs.title: Dims and their policies
docs.text:
The policy is the heart of the contract: it says what a score request may do with a dim.

Policy For At score time Typical errors fixed channels, products, states Only labels seen at fit (any subset, any order) UNSEEN_LEVELS extend time, observation index New labels appended after the fitted range, without gaps, up to max_extension NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION, COORD_NOT_ALLOWED, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT new_levels markets, stores, counties, households Unseen labels allowed, handled by new_level_strategy UNSEEN_LEVELS when the strategy is error

new_level_strategy decides what an unseen level becomes:

Strategy Meaning Example hyperprior A fresh draw from the fitted population distribution, per posterior draw A new market in a hierarchical MMM: honest, wider uncertainty pooled The population average (or a frequency-weighted average of fitted levels) A new store in an xgboost demand model zero The level contributes nothing A new category in a one-hot model error Rejected The default

Other DimSpec fields:

  • kind: categorical, time, integer, float or index;
  • freq: a pandas frequency for time dims (D, W-SUN, MS), so the platform can generate forecast coordinates and check contiguity;
  • max_extension: how many periods a forecast may reach past the fit without a refit;
  • ordered: whether a categorical dim has a meaningful order.

Policies only tighten

A model's schema template declares the loosest policy it can handle; your data's schema and the spec's dim_policies may only make it tighter (fixed is the tightest). Trying to loosen it is DIM_POLICY_LOOSENED.

docs.title: Variables and roles
docs.text:
Field Meaning dims, dtype The shape contract (float64, int64, bool, str, datetime64[ns], …) role What the variable means: target, covariate, media, spend, control, index, mask, constant, weight, exposure units A pint-style string (EUR, units, 1). Steps update it (fx_convert → EUR, scaling → 1), and outputs report it missing forbid (default), allow (NaN is fine) or mask (a mask variable marks valid cells) missing_sentinel A code such as -99.99 that means "missing" and is turned into NaN by core.replace_sentinel future_required Must be supplied over a forecast horizon (planned prices, promotions, budgets) index_of Long layout: this integer variable indexes that dim (county_idx(obs) → county) bounds Allowed value range, checked in plain language

Roles let plugins and plot templates work across datasets: "every spend variable", "the target over time, one line per geo".

docs.title: Two layouts for ragged data
docs.text:
Real panels are often ragged: households have different numbers of trips, animals different track lengths. A schema uses one of two canonical forms, and the built-in steps core.to_long and core.to_padded convert between them.

LongPadded

One row per observation along an obs dim, plus index variables:

layout: long
dims:
  obs:    {kind: integer, policy: extend}
  county: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
vars:
  log_radon:  {dims: [obs], dtype: float64, role: target}
  county_idx: {dims: [obs], dtype: int64, role: index, index_of: county}

A dense cube plus a mask variable:

dims:
  animal: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: pooled}
  step:   {kind: integer, policy: extend}
vars:
  y:    {dims: [animal, step], dtype: float64, role: target, missing: mask}
  mask: {dims: [animal, step], dtype: bool, role: mask}
ragged:
  - {group_dim: animal, within_dim: step, form: padded, mask_var: mask}

docs.title: Draft a schema from data
docs.text:
infer_schema gives you a starting point: time dims become extend with an inferred frequency, other dims fixed, variables covariate unless you say otherwise.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from mapi_sdk import infer_schema, validate_dataset
from mapi_spec import DimPolicy

days = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=28, freq="D")
markets = ["DE", "FR", "UK"]
channels = ["tv", "search"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
media = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "revenue": (("market", "date"), rng.gamma(50.0, 20.0, (3, 28))),
        "spend": (("market", "channel", "date"), rng.gamma(5.0, 100.0, (3, 2, 28))),
    },
    coords={"market": markets, "channel": channels, "date": days},
)

schema = infer_schema(
    media,
    targets=["revenue"],
    policies={"market": "new_levels"},
    units={"revenue": "EUR", "spend": "EUR"},
)
print(schema.dims["date"].policy, schema.dims["date"].freq)  # extend D
print(schema.dims["channel"].policy)  # fixed
print(schema.vars["revenue"].role)  # target

docs.title: Data checks in plain language
docs.text:
validate_dataset checks a dataset against its schema and describes every problem for a non-expert reader. Fitting and scoring run the same checks and stop on errors.

broken = media.copy(deep=True)
broken["revenue"].loc[{"market": ["FR", "UK"], "date": days[10:12]}] = np.nan

for issue in validate_dataset(schema, broken):
    print(issue.severity, issue.code, "-", issue.message)
# error SCHEMA_INVALID - 2 markets are missing 2 days of revenue in March 2026

docs.title: Binding: your names, the model's names
docs.text:
Steps and models are written against canonical names (geo, time, y, spend). A spec's data.bind maps them to your dataset's names. The binding is stored in the bundle and reversed on every output, so results come back in your vocabulary.

from mapi_sdk import BindingMap

binding = BindingMap({"dims": {"geo": "market", "time": "date"}, "vars": {"y": "revenue"}})
canonical = binding.apply(media)  # what steps and models see
print(sorted(canonical.dims))  # ['channel', 'geo', 'time']
print(sorted(binding.reverse(canonical).dims))  # ['channel', 'date', 'market'] - your names

data:
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, time: date}     # canonical: yours
    vars: {y: revenue, spend: spend}

docs.title: Side tables
docs.text:
Small constant datasets that steps read (FX rates, holiday calendars) are side tables, declared in the spec with a score-time policy:

score_policy At score time pinned The exact version used at fit time (holidays) latest The latest version of the table supplied The score request must name the table (request.side_tables), e.g. FX rates for the forecast period

A step that needs a table with too little coverage fails with SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE.

docs.title: Wire formats
docs.text:
Format Use API XrJSON Small payloads, curl, TypeScript: the Dataset.to_dict() shape with explicit dtypes and caps mapi_sdk.wire.to_xrjson / from_xrjson zarr zip Datasets and trees as single objects (zarr v3, deterministic bytes, zstd/blosc only) write_zarr_zip, read_zarr_zip, write_datatree_zip, read_datatree_zip Arrow IPC Tidy tables for UI views and plots mapi_sdk.wire.to_arrow_table pickle Never, across any boundary –

Next: Pipelines and stages.

docs.title: Pipelines, stages and replay
docs.text:
A pipeline is an ordered list of steps. Each step is a small, versioned transform with typed settings and, if it learns something, a fitted state. The promise of the platform is simple to state and fiddly to keep:

Scoring replays exactly the preprocessing that was learned at fit time. It never refits.

This page explains the pieces that keep that promise: stages, the split stage, context tails, inverse transforms and scenario entry points.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
A step implements fit (learn, on train only), transform (apply; never learns) and, when it can, inverse. A complete one, from the porting guide:

A scaling step, in full 
from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sdk import Step, StepContext, StepSettings, StepState
from mapi_spec import StepKind
from pydantic import Field, JsonValue


class ScaleSettings(StepSettings):
    vars: list[str]
    over: list[str] = Field(default=[])  # plain defaults: the exported JSON Schema keeps them
    unseen_levels: str = "error"  # error | pooled | fill: what a new level's scale becomes
    fill_value: float = 1.0  # the scale used by 'fill'


class ScaleStep(Step[ScaleSettings, StepState]):
    """Divide each variable by its mean absolute value over `over` (learned on train)."""

    id = "acme.scale"
    version = "1.0.0"
    kind = StepKind.VALUE
    Settings = ScaleSettings
    State = StepState  # stateful: fitted on the training data only
    invertible = True
    var_params = ("vars",)  # settings that name variables ...
    dim_params = ("over",)  # ... and dims, so the control plane can check them
    unseen_levels_param = "unseen_levels"
    effect_template: ClassVar[dict[str, JsonValue]] = {  # static: how the schema changes
        "template_params": ["vars"],
        "updates": {"{*vars as v}": {"units": "1"}},
    }
    summary = "Divide by the mean absolute value over the named dims"  # catalog and UI text
    summary_plain = "Puts each series on a comparable scale"

    def fit(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, ctx: StepContext) -> StepState:
        return StepState(arrays=xr.Dataset({f"scale__{v}": abs(ds[v]).mean(s.over) for v in s.vars}))

    def _scale(self, v: str, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, st: StepState, ctx: StepContext):
        state = st.array(f"scale__{v}")
        return ctx.align_state(state, ds, s.unseen_levels, fill_value=s.fill_value)

    def transform(self, ds, s, st, ctx):  # never learns; skips absent vars (the target at score)
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] / self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

    def inverse(self, ds, s, st, ctx):
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] * self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

Every step has a kind:

Kind Changes Inverted on the way out? Examples reshape Structure: dims, frequency, layout Never resample, to_long, stack, filter_coords value Values of existing variables Yes, if invertible fx_convert, mean_scale, standardize, log1p feature Adds new variables Not needed lag, fourier, calendar, one_hot, formula

And a static schema effect: a JSON template that says how the step changes the schema (adds lag dim, sets units to 1, turns daily date into weekly time). The control plane uses it to propagate the schema through the whole pipeline without running anything.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
A stage is the dataset after a named step; raw is the bound input. Static validation computes the schema at every stage, so problems surface before any data is read:

from mapi_plugin_mmm.examples import E33_SPEC_YAML, e33_dataset, e33_raw_schema
from mapi_sdk import default_registry
from mapi_spec import load_model_spec, validate_spec

catalog = default_registry().catalog()  # static JSON: settings schemas + schema effects
data, _ = e33_dataset(weeks=12)
raw_schema = e33_raw_schema(data)

check = validate_spec(load_model_spec(E33_SPEC_YAML), catalog, raw_schema)
rs = check.resolved
for stage, schema in rs.stages.items():
    y, time = schema.vars["y"], schema.dims["time"]
    print(f"{stage:12} time={time.freq:6} y in {y.units:4} dims={', '.join(schema.dims)}")
# raw          time=D      y in LCU  dims=geo, channel, time
# to_eur       time=D      y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# weekly       time=W-SUN  y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# scale_spend  time=W-SUN  y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# scale_y      time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time
# lags         time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag
# season       time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag, fourier_mode
# hols         time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag, fourier_mode
print(rs.split_stage)  # weekly: the holdout is cut in whole weeks
print(rs.last_reshape_stage)  # weekly: outputs are inverted back to weekly EUR, not days

Stages are how specs refer to points in the pipeline:

  • data.split.after_step: where the train/holdout split happens;
  • ScoreRequest.inputs_stage: where a scenario enters the pipeline;
  • the output space: the stage outputs are inverted back to.

docs.title: Where the split happens
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["raw<br/>daily, LCU"] --> FX["to_eur<br/><i>stateless</i>"]
    FX --> W["weekly<br/><i>stateless reshape</i>"]
    W --> SPLIT{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
    SPLIT -->|train| SC["scale_spend, scale_y<br/><i>learn on train</i>"]
    SPLIT -.->|holdout| SC
    SC --> L["lags<br/><i>context tail</i>"]
    L --> M["model"]
    style SPLIT fill:#5eead4,stroke:#0f766e,color:#1e1b4b

Some dims only exist after preprocessing: a holdout of "the last 8 weeks" cannot be cut from daily data before it is resampled. So the split happens at a stage. If after_step is not given, it defaults to the end of the stateless prefix, the leading steps that learn nothing (unit conversion, resampling).

If a step that learns runs before the split, its state would be learned partly from the holdout and the evaluation would be optimistic. Validation reports it:

leaky = E33_SPEC_YAML.replace("after_step: weekly", "after_step: scale_y")
for issue in validate_spec(load_model_spec(leaky), catalog, raw_schema).errors:
    print(issue.code, issue.pointer)
    print("  ", issue.message)
# LEAKAGE_RISK /data/split/after_step
#    stateful step 'scale_spend' (pipeline[2]) runs before the split at stage 'scale_y';
#    its state would be learned from holdout data
# LEAKAGE_RISK /data/split/after_step
#    stateful step 'scale_y' (pipeline[3]) runs before the split at stage 'scale_y'; ...

Set allow_leakage: true on the split to downgrade the error to an acknowledged warning.

docs.title: Evaluate the way you will forecast
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit (the default) does this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Data
    participant P as Pipeline + model
    participant B as Bundles
    D->>P: stateless prefix on all data, then split at the split stage
    P->>P: fit step states + model on TRAIN
    P->>P: score HOLDOUT through the score path<br/>(context tails from train)
    P->>B: evaluation bundle + metrics
    P->>P: refit states + model on ALL data
    P->>B: production bundle (links evaluation + metrics)

The holdout is never scored by a separate code path: it goes through score_bundle, with the context it would have in production. Then everything is refitted on all data, so the context tails and terminal states that forecasts start from are the latest ones. train_only stops after evaluation and keeps the train fit.

docs.title: Context tails: looking back across the fit boundary
docs.text:
Steps that look back in time (lags, carry-over) declare a context need, for example {along: time, n: 6, within: [geo]}. At fit time the step stores the last n rows of its own input stage, per group. At score time the platform prepends them before transforming, checks that the new data continues the fitted range, and drops them from the output.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Fit
        T1["… w49 w50 w51 w52"] --> TAIL["stored tail per geo:<br/>w47–w52 (weekly, scaled)"]
    end
    subgraph Score
        TAIL --> CAT["w47–w52 ‖ w53 w54 w55 w56"]
        NEW["forecast payload<br/>w53–w56"] --> CAT
        CAT --> LAG["lag_tensor"] --> DROP["drop context rows"] --> OUT["w53–w56 with<br/>real carry-over"]
    end

The result is identical to transforming the whole series at once; the contract kit checks this "context-window equivalence" for every step and model. A new market has no tail, so its lags are padded according to the step's settings (pad: first).

Sequential models (HMMs, Kalman filters) keep a model-side terminal state instead; see Forecasting.

docs.title: Inverse transforms and the output space
docs.text:
On the way out, the platform undoes invertible value steps in reverse order and stops at the last reshape step. A model fitted on weekly, scaled EUR returns weekly EUR: scaling can be undone, the weekly resample cannot (daily values are not recoverable from weekly sums).

Every output records where it ended up:

Attribute Example Meaning output_space {"y_hat": "weekly"} The stage the values live at units EUR Units after inversion retransform {"y_hat": "median"} For point models through a non-linear inverse: the inverse of a mean is not a mean, so the value is labelled (or Duan smearing is used)

Ask for output: {units: model} to skip inversion, for example to get contributions that add up exactly through a log1p.

docs.title: Scenarios enter at a stage
docs.text:
A planner should not have to invent daily local-currency spend to ask about a weekly EUR budget. ScoreRequest.inputs_stage lets data enter the pipeline after a named step; the steps before it, and the side tables they need, are skipped:

mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 8}
inputs_stage: weekly        # send weekly EUR spend; to_eur and the FX table are skipped

The E33 conformance fixture checks that this gives exactly the same forecast as the raw daily path for the same spend.

docs.title: Models that own their preprocessing
docs.text: Some models do their own scaling or carry-over (pymc-marketing's MMM does both). They declare owns: [scaling, carryover, inverse_units] in their capabilities, the platform steps aside, and outputs are labelled as already in original units. See the pymc-marketing adapter.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
A lag of the target is a recursive feature: forecasting more periods than the smallest lag would need predictions as inputs. v1 forecasts are direct, so such specs are rejected with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED unless the model declares owns: [recursion].

Next: Representations and summaries.

docs.title: Representations and summaries
docs.text:
"One output shape for every model" sounds tidy and is quietly wrong. A conformal interval is not a distribution; per-cell quantiles cannot be added up; a point prediction has no uncertainty to summarise. So every model declares its representation, and the platform uses it to decide which summaries and aggregations it will compute.

Representation Shape Typical models Summaries Aggregate over cells draws (chain, draw, …) joint samples PyMC (MCMC, VI), bootstrap mean, sd, median, hdi_<p>, eti_<p>, q<p> any, per draw quantiles (quantile, …) per cell xgboost / sklearn quantile regression median, q<p>, eti_<p>, point (interpolated, never extrapolated) none interval (bound, …) + alpha split conformal interval, point none point (…) ridge, random forest, classifiers mean, point sum/mean, flagged moments (moment, …) mean and sd analytic Gaussian processes mean, sd, eti_<p>, point none

docs.title: Why aggregation depends on it
docs.text:
With joint draws the total over 40 stores is easy and exact: add the stores within each draw, then summarise. With quantiles you cannot do that: the sum of 40 90% quantiles is not the 90% quantile of the sum (it overstates it, often badly), and the quantiles say nothing about how stores co-vary. Conformal intervals guarantee per-cell coverage only; a "summed interval" would claim a coverage nobody measured.

The rules are data, in mapi_spec, and the summariser and the API both use them:

from mapi_spec import Representation, can_aggregate, default_summary, summary_allowed

for rep in Representation:
    verdict = can_aggregate(rep, ["store"], how="sum")
    print(f"{rep.value:10} sum over stores: {verdict.allowed!s:5} default summary: {default_summary(rep)}")
# draws      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['mean', 'hdi_90']
# quantiles  sum over stores: False default summary: ['median', 'q5', 'q95']
# interval   sum over stores: False default summary: ['point', 'interval']
# point      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['point']
# moments    sum over stores: False default summary: ['mean', 'sd']

print(can_aggregate(Representation.POINT, ["store"]).flagged)  # True: allowed, but labelled
print(can_aggregate(Representation.QUANTILES, ["store"]).reason)
# Quantiles are marginal per cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.
print(summary_allowed(Representation.QUANTILES, "hdi_90"))  # False: no draws to find an HDI
print(summary_allowed(Representation.DRAWS, "q97_5"))  # True

Asking for something the representation cannot support fails before any compute:

CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED - cannot aggregate 'quantiles' output: Quantiles are marginal per
cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.

docs.title: Asking for outputs
docs.text:
A score request's output block is an OutputSelector:

output:
  kind: expected              # expected (the mean response) or predictive (with noise)
  summary: [mean, hdi_90]     # default depends on the representation
  draws: 200                  # also return 200 joint draws (draws representation only)
  aggregate: {over: [store]}  # reduce before summarising, if the representation allows
  units: original             # or: model (skip inverse transforms)
  names: dataset              # or: canonical (skip reverse binding)

Summary names are parsed, not looked up: hdi_90, eti_80, q5, q97_5, median, sd. When you leave summary unset you get the representation's default (mean, hdi_90 for draws, median, q5, q95 for quantiles, adapted to the fitted quantile grid).

docs.title: Expected vs predictive
docs.text:
• expected returns the model's mean response (for PyMC models, a Deterministic the plugin names), without observation noise. Use it for "what is the effect of the plan?".
  • predictive returns draws of the observed variable, with noise. Use it for "what range of sales should we plan for?".

docs.title: Draws are thinned once, for the whole bundle
docs.text: When a request asks for draws, they come from a bundle-wide thinning index: the same (chain, draw) pairs for every output and every derived quantity. Contributions, response curves and predictions taken from the same draws stay jointly consistent, so a Guided-mode slider that combines them keeps honest uncertainty bands.

docs.title: Counterfactuals share their noise
docs.text:
In mode: counterfactual the platform scores a baseline and a scenario and returns baseline/ and delta/ groups. Bayesian plugins use common random numbers: the predictive noise of the two runs is the same draw, so the delta reflects the intervention, not two independent noise samples.

Next: Bundles.

docs.title: Security model v0.2
docs.text:
modeling-api is built to run models and data from people it does not trust, eventually from the public internet. v0.2 is a single-tenant, local slice of that platform, but the controls that do not depend on the cloud are already in the code and tested, so the design is exercised from the first release. This page says what each control protects against and how much of it you get in each setting.

v0.2 has no authentication

The API, the web app and the object store listen on 127.0.0.1, and Docker Compose publishes its ports on 127.0.0.1 only. Anyone who can reach those ports can do anything. Do not expose a v0.2 stack to a network you do not trust, and do not run untrusted plugin code on it: local and compose runs are not a multi-tenant boundary.

docs.title: What it protects
docs.text: Asset Threat Main controls The control plane A hostile dataset, bundle or plot exploits a parser in the API The API parses JSON and YAML only (a strict loader: no anchors or tags, size and depth caps). Arrays, zarr, netCDF, CSV and Parquet are opened only inside a run's sandbox Credentials and other runs Model code reads or steals what the run holds Supervisor/worker split; no secrets in the environment or arguments; a one-time bootstrap object; object-scoped, short-lived signed URLs Results A run forges outputs, swaps an object later, or fakes progress Outputs are claims checked against the store's own checksums and generations; write-once bundles; signed bundle manifests checked before every download link; HMAC-signed events The browser and the user's data A malicious plot spec runs script in the app A server-side sanitizer, then rendering only in a sandboxed iframe on a separate origin, with strict CSPs on both origins The user's terminal and screen Log lines or messages with escape codes, HTML or bidi tricks Untrusted text is a separate field (untrusted_text), stripped of ANSI, control and bidi characters, and rendered as text only Long-term trust in a model Pickle and other code-executing formats Bundles are zarr zips plus JSON; native models are skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON; pickle is refused on write and on read

docs.title: Local development vs production
docs.text: Control make dev (v0.2) Docker Compose (v0.2) Production (v0.3 and later) Authentication None; 127.0.0.1 only None; ports published on 127.0.0.1 only OIDC for people, scoped API tokens with budgets for programs Tenancy One tenant and project (default); every row and storage key already carries them Same Multiple tenants; PostgreSQL row-level security on every table Run isolation A separate worker process with a scrubbed environment, as your own user (DEV_MODE_ISOLATION) local-process: as above, inside a hardened container. docker executor: one container per run, read-only root, no-new-privileges, the supervisor with only the capabilities the uid split needs and the worker as uid 10001 with none (MAPI_REQUIRE_ISOLATION) A fresh Cloud Run Jobs microVM per run; the worker under its own uid with no_new_privs; read-only root Network egress from runs Not restricted docker executor: the GCS shim's network namespace, or an internal network containing only the shim Deny-all egress, including DNS, inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter Object storage permissions The GCS shim enforces per-principal permissions: runs' credentials can only get and delete their bootstrap object Same Cloud Storage IAM; the same layout and principals Bundle signatures EC P-256 with a local key in .local/keys/ EC P-256 with one key on the keys volume, created by migrate and mounted read-only into api and worker Cloud KMS, same signed bytes Event integrity HMAC per event, read from the supervisor's stdout pipe Same HMAC per event, through Cloud Logging and Pub/Sub with OIDC push Web app CSP The Vite dev server does not send the app's CSP (hot reload needs inline scripts); the plot sandbox's CSP is enforced Enforced by nginx, with Trusted Types in report-only mode Enforced Plot isolation Separate origin (port 5174), sandbox="allow-scripts" Separate origin (port 5174) Separate domain (plots.<domain>) Quotas and cost limits None Worker memory, CPU and /tmp limits Per-tenant and per-token vCPU-second quotas, priority classes, a global kill switch

docs.title: The run sandbox
docs.text:
Every run is a pair of processes started by an executor that passes only the run id and a 256-bit nonce. The trusted supervisor uses the nonce to fetch its instructions (signed URLs for its inputs and outputs, an event HMAC key, limits) from a one-time bootstrap object, and deletes it before any model code starts; the storage credential it used can get and delete bootstrap objects and do nothing else, not even list them. The worker that runs the SDK and the plugin gets an allow-listed environment with every MAPI_* variable removed, its own session, and (where the supervisor starts as root) a separate uid with no_new_privs and no core dumps. It can only talk to the supervisor, in schema-checked frames.

On a laptop the supervisor is not root, so the worker runs as you: the run reports DEV_MODE_ISOLATION. Everything else (the split, the scrubbed environment, signed events, caps, output verification) still applies, but the boundary between your account and the model code is only as strong as Python's process separation. Treat local runs like running the plugin in a notebook.

docs.title: Outputs are claims
docs.text: A run can only write under its own attempt prefix, through a POST policy with a size range. When it finishes, the control plane does not read its outputs; it lists them and compares the size, CRC32C, MD5 and generation the store computed with the run's signed manifest. Any missing, changed or extra object fails the run with INTEGRITY_FAILURE and raises an alert. Verified objects are copied server-side into a write-once bundles bucket the runs cannot reach, and a bundle manifest binding the tenant, run, hashes and every destination generation is signed. Download links are minted only after that signature verifies, and each link is pinned to an object generation and expires after 15 minutes. Deleting the signing key (.local/keys/) therefore makes existing model versions undownloadable, by design.

docs.title: Events and liveness
docs.text: Only the supervisor writes the real stdout. Each event line carries a sequence number and an HMAC under the run's key; the control plane verifies it in constant time, deduplicates on (run, attempt, seq) and drops forged lines (counting them as sandbox violations). Events never decide whether a run is alive: the executor's own status does, so a run cannot keep itself "running" by talking, or get itself killed by going quiet.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
Plot specs come from recipes, plugins and, later, users, and Vega and Plotly are large JavaScript libraries. So:

  1. The server sanitizes every spec when a run finishes and again on every read: pinned Vega-Lite and Plotly schemas, no URL data, no href encodings, no external images, no tile maps, no prototype keys, Plotly HTML reduced to b, i, br, sub, sup, and size and depth caps.
  2. Every plot renders in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> (no allow-same-origin) from the plot sandbox's origin, with default-src 'none', scripts from its own origin only, connect-src limited to its own topojson, and frame-ancestors set to the app.
  3. Vega runs with the expression interpreter (no eval), a loader that rejects every URL and a text-only tooltip; Plotly uses its strict bundle.
  4. The app and the sandbox exchange a small, validated postMessage protocol; the app accepts messages only from that iframe's window with an opaque origin.

The remaining risk (a sandboxed frame could navigate itself and leak the data posted into it) is accepted only for a viewer's own data; shared and embedded plots (v0.4) render platform recipes only.

docs.title: Untrusted text
docs.text: Log lines, tracebacks and plugin messages travel in untrusted_text or LogLine.line, never in detail. The runner strips ANSI, control and bidi characters; the web app renders them as text (ESLint forbids dangerouslySetInnerHTML); Monaco hovers are untrusted; the CLI strips escape sequences before printing.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
• Python dependencies are locked with hashes in uv.lock; container images are built from the lock with --frozen, and base images are pinned by digest (make docker-pin-check).
  • Build-time guards fail an image that contains what it must not: no numpy, xarray, PyMC, SDK or plugin in the control-plane image, and the import-linter contracts run against the installed packages inside the server image build.
  • The web image installs JavaScript dependencies with --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts.
  • This documentation site's OpenAPI explorer loads a vendored, hash-pinned Redoc bundle; it makes no request outside the site.

Known gaps in v0.2

  • The API's built-in /docs and /redoc pages (FastAPI's defaults) load Swagger UI and Redoc from a public CDN. Use the OpenAPI explorer or /openapi.json instead.
  • The app's CSP is not enforced by the Vite dev server (see the table).
  • Local and compose runs have no egress restriction unless you use the docker executor.
  • Under the local-process executor, run code runs as the orchestrator's own uid, so it can read the shim's control key and the bundle-signing key. The orchestrator is non-dumpable and logs a warning at start-up, but run only trusted plugin code in this mode; see Docker Compose.

docs.title: What production adds
docs.text: v0.3 moves runs to Cloud Run Jobs: a fresh microVM per run, a separate execution project with deny-all egress (DNS included) and VPC Service Controls, a bootstrap bucket the execution service account can only get from and delete in, Cloud KMS signatures, OIDC, scoped tokens, row-level security, quotas and a kill switch. Public code upload comes only after a dedicated overlay build pipeline, abuse controls and an external penetration test.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
There are two ways to use modeling-api, and they share everything: the spec format, the steps, the models and the bundles.

  • Run the platform v0.2

    Start the API, the job queue, the sandboxed runner and the web app on your laptop with make dev, then fit and score from the browser, the CLI, Python or HTTP.

    Quickstart: zero to first model in 10 minutes

  • Use the library in your own process

    import mapi_sdk in a notebook, a script or a test suite: validate specs, fit, score and write bundles in-process, and test your own plugins with the contract kit.

    Your first model in Python

Both need Python 3.12 and uv. The platform also needs Node.js 22+ with pnpm for the web app; Docker is optional (Deployment).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From a clone (today)Into your own project (once published)

The packages are developed together in one uv workspace. Clone the repository and sync every package plus the developer tools:

git clone <repository-url> modeling-api
cd modeling-api
uv sync --all-packages        # or: make install (also installs the web app)
uv run python -c "import mapi_sdk, mapi_spec; print(mapi_sdk.__version__)"

Open a notebook in the same environment with uv run --with jupyterlab jupyter lab.

Each package is a separate distribution, so you install only what you need:

uv add mapi-sdk mapi-steps                 # the runtime and the built-in steps
uv add mapi-pymc                           # PyMC models
uv add mapi-sklearn                        # scikit-learn and xgboost models
uv add "mapi-plots[recipes]"               # plot recipes (Altair, Plotly)
uv add mapi-plugin-mmm mapi-plugin-ts mapi-plugin-tabular   # the built-in models

Not on PyPI yet

The distributions are published with the first tagged release. Until then, install from the workspace as shown in the first tab.

docs.title: What each package does
docs.text:
Package Import What it gives you Heavy dependencies mapi-spec mapi_spec The contracts: DataSchema, ModelSpec, ScoreRequest, capabilities, error codes, static validation, JSON Schemas none (pure Pydantic) mapi-sdk mapi_sdk The runtime: steps, pipelines, coord plans, summaries, bundles, the in-process executor and the contract kit xarray, numpy, zarr mapi-steps mapi_steps 28 built-in preprocessing steps and the split catalog – mapi-pymc mapi_pymc PyMCModel: write build(), get engines, diagnostics, new levels and counterfactuals PyMC mapi-sklearn mapi_sklearn SklearnModel: write estimator(), get stacking, safe persistence and uncertainty scikit-learn, xgboost, skops mapi-plots mapi_plots The JSON-only plot sanitizer and templates; recipes with the recipes extra Altair, Plotly (extra) mapi-plugin-* mapi_plugin_* Built-in models: marketing mix, time series, tabular as above mapi-conformance mapi_conformance The conformance corpus and its runner all of the above mapi-client mapi_client Typed Python client for the HTTP API (guide) httpx (xarray optional) mapi-cli mapi_cli The mapi command line (guide) typer, rich mapi-server mapi_server The control plane: API, orchestrator, executors (AGPL or commercial) FastAPI, SQLAlchemy; no numpy mapi-runner mapi_runner The sandboxed run harness: supervisor and worker (AGPL or commercial) the SDK, in the worker only mapi-gcs-shim mapi_gcs_shim A local emulator of the Cloud Storage features the platform uses Starlette

Plugins register themselves through Python entry points (mapi.steps, mapi.models, mapi.plots), so mapi_sdk.default_registry() finds everything that is installed.

docs.text:
uv run python -m mapi_conformance list          # the reference problems
make conformance FIXTURE=xgb_store_demand       # one of them, end to end (a few seconds)

xgb_store_demand  tabular.regressor@1.0.0  ok        ok   ok 6/6  ok        ok 12/12  ok 3/3  ok            coverage_80=0.825, mape=25.3, rmse=4.59  3.3s  PASS
